title: Age-related macular degeneration (NICE guideline NG82)
text: NG82 advises that people with suspected late AMD (wet active) are referred urgently to a macular service, normally within 1 working day, whether or not they report visual impairment. Emergency referral is not needed. Treatment with anti VEGF should start as soon as possible, within 14 days of referral to the macular service, for eyes with confirmed late AMD (wet active) where antiangiogenic treatment is recommended. Late AMD (wet active) is suspected clinically and confirmed with optical coherence tomography, with fluorescein angiography added if OCT does not exclude neovascular disease. Early and late dry AMD are confirmed by slit lamp biomicroscopic examination of the fundus. The guideline also describes late AMD (wet inactive), which is monitored rather than treated. Anti VEGF treatment is offered for late AMD (wet active) in eyes with best corrected visual acuity of 6/12 to 6/96, in line with the technology appraisals for ranibizumab, aflibercept and later agents, which also require no permanent structural damage to the central fovea, a lesion of 12 disc areas or less in greatest linear dimension and evidence of recent presumed disease progression. NG82 extends treatment to eyes with acuity better than 6/12, which it found clinically effective and potentially cost effective depending on the regimen. For eyes with acuity of 6/96 or worse, anti VEGF treatment should be considered only when an overall benefit to visual function is expected, for example when the affected eye is the better seeing eye. The appraised agents are considered clinically equivalent, so the least expensive overall option is preferred. Bevacizumab is not licensed for intraocular use in the UK. Where it is used, the prescriber takes full responsibility for the decision and informed consent must be obtained and documented. NG82 advises considering stopping anti VEGF treatment when the eye has severe, progressive visual loss despite treatment, and stopping when the eye develops late AMD (wet inactive) with no prospect of functional improvement. Switching between anti VEGF agents may be considered for practical reasons, but clinical benefit from switching is likely to be limited. Observation may be considered when disease appears stable. People should be involved in every decision to stop or switch treatment. Photodynamic therapy should not be offered alone for late AMD (wet active), and should not be offered as a first line adjunct to anti VEGF; as a second line adjunct it should be offered only within a randomised controlled trial. Intravitreal corticosteroids should not be offered as an adjunct to anti VEGF, and thermal laser should not be offered for drusen in early AMD. For people with late AMD (wet active), ongoing OCT monitoring of both eyes is offered, and people monitored for late AMD (wet inactive) have both eyes reviewed at each appointment.

title: Glaucoma: diagnosis and management (NICE guideline NG81)
text: The 2022 update of NG81 recommends 360 degree selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) as the first treatment for people with newly diagnosed ocular hypertension (OHT) or chronic open angle glaucoma (COAG), replacing the 2017 recommendation of prostaglandin analogue eye drops first. For ocular hypertension the treatment recommendation applies to people with an intraocular pressure of 24 mmHg or more who are at risk of visual impairment within their lifetime. SLT is not recommended first where glaucoma or ocular hypertension is associated with pigment dispersion syndrome, where eye drops are considered more suitable. Generic prostaglandin analogue eye drops are offered to people who prefer not to have 360 degree SLT or for whom it is not suitable, and the drop instillation technique should be demonstrated and checked by observation when drops are first prescribed. A second 360 degree SLT may be offered at the discretion of the consultant ophthalmologist if the effect of the first treatment wears off and pressure rises. NG81 considered that SLT would generally need to work for at least 6 months to be regarded as successful, while allowing clinical discretion. People suitable for SLT are referred to a consultant ophthalmologist, and staff performing SLT need appropriate training and support.

title: Cataracts in adults: management (NICE guideline NG77)
text: NG77 advises that referral for cataract surgery should be based on the impact of the cataract on the person's vision and quality of life rather than on a visual acuity threshold, after discussion of the benefits and risks of surgery. The guideline evidence review compared intraocular lens power formulae in network meta analyses grouped by axial length. Differences between formulae were mostly small with overlapping credible intervals; the largest evidence base concerned eyes shorter than 22.00 mm, and in the 22.00 to 24.50 mm range SRK/T ranked first for mean absolute error in only two studies. Formula choice therefore remains a matter for the local biometry protocol.

Pegaptanib is not recommended.

title: Brolucizumab for treating wet age-related macular degeneration
text: TA672, published in February 2021, recommends brolucizumab for wet age related macular degeneration in adults only if the eye has best corrected visual acuity between 6/12 and 6/96, no permanent structural damage to the central fovea, a lesion of 12 disc areas or less in greatest linear dimension and recent disease progression, and the company provides it under the commercial arrangement. If brolucizumab, aflibercept and ranibizumab are all suitable, the least expensive should be chosen. Treatment should continue only while an adequate response is maintained, and should stop with persistent deterioration in vision or anatomical changes showing an inadequate response.

title: Faricimab for treating diabetic macular oedema
